principles.name: Name the failure model
principles.body: Every design should state what it tolerates: how many node crashes, which partitions, how much clock skew, whether disks can lie about fsync. Undocumented assumptions become production incidents.
principles.html: Every design should state what it tolerates: how many node crashes, which partitions, how much clock skew, whether disks can lie about fsync. Undocumented assumptions become production incidents.

principles.name: Safety unconditional, liveness conditional
principles.body: Prefer designs that may stall under bad conditions but never corrupt or lose committed data. Make stalls observable and recoverable.
principles.html: Prefer designs that may stall under bad conditions but never corrupt or lose committed data. Make stalls observable and recoverable.

principles.name: Buy the weakest consistency that is correct, and document it
principles.body: Strong consistency where a stale read causes a wrong decision (money, uniqueness, permissions, leadership); session guarantees or eventual consistency elsewhere. Write down which is which per API.
principles.html: Strong consistency where a stale read causes a wrong decision (money, uniqueness, permissions, leadership); session guarantees or eventual consistency elsewhere. Write down which is which per API.

principles.name: Never use wall-clock time for correctness without a bound
principles.body: Use monotonic clocks for durations, logical or hybrid clocks for ordering, fencing tokens for exclusion, and an enforced maximum skew wherever time remains in the critical path.
principles.html: Use monotonic clocks for durations, logical or hybrid clocks for ordering, fencing tokens for exclusion, and an enforced maximum skew wherever time remains in the critical path.

principles.name: Every write path is idempotent
principles.body: Assume every message will be delivered at least twice and every request retried. Design keys, conditional writes, and dedup records accordingly.
principles.html: Assume every message will be delivered at least twice and every request retried. Design keys, conditional writes, and dedup records accordingly.

principles.name: Bound everything
principles.body: Queues, retries, timeouts, concurrency, batch sizes, cache sizes, fan-out, and payloads. An unbounded resource is a future outage with an unknown trigger.
principles.html: Queues, retries, timeouts, concurrency, batch sizes, cache sizes, fan-out, and payloads. An unbounded resource is a future outage with an unknown trigger.

principles.name: Fail fast and shed early
principles.body: A quick rejection is cheaper for everyone than a slow failure. Reject at the edge, before expensive work.
principles.html: A quick rejection is cheaper for everyone than a slow failure. Reject at the edge, before expensive work.

principles.name: Retry at one layer, with jitter and a budget
principles.body: Multiplicative retries turn partial outages into total ones.
principles.html: Multiplicative retries turn partial outages into total ones.

principles.name: Make the common transaction single-partition
principles.body: Choose partition keys that align with the dominant access and transaction boundary. Cross-partition coordination should be the exception.
principles.html: Choose partition keys that align with the dominant access and transaction boundary. Cross-partition coordination should be the exception.

principles.name: Count failure domains, not replicas
principles.body: Replicas that share power, network, software version, configuration, or deployment wave are one replica for correlated failures.
principles.html: Replicas that share power, network, software version, configuration, or deployment wave are one replica for correlated failures.

principles.name: Detect from the client's point of view
principles.body: Health checks that exercise trivial paths miss gray failures. Measure what users experience and alert on it.
principles.html: Health checks that exercise trivial paths miss gray failures. Measure what users experience and alert on it.

principles.name: Fence the past
principles.body: Every leader, lease, and configuration has an epoch. Stale actors must be rejected by the resource they touch, not trusted to know they are stale.
principles.html: Every leader, lease, and configuration has an epoch. Stale actors must be rejected by the resource they touch, not trusted to know they are stale.

principles.name: Keep consensus small
principles.body: Put metadata, leases, and configuration in a consensus system; keep bulk data and hot paths out of it.
principles.html: Put metadata, leases, and configuration in a consensus system; keep bulk data and hot paths out of it.

principles.name: Design the recovery path, not just the steady state
principles.body: Cold caches, rebuilds, rebalances, and restarts are when systems are most fragile. Rate-limit them and test them.
principles.html: Cold caches, rebuilds, rebalances, and restarts are when systems are most fragile. Rate-limit them and test them.

principles.name: Prefer static stability
principles.body: During a dependency failure, a system should keep doing what it was doing (serve last known config, keep existing capacity) rather than needing the failed dependency to recover.
principles.html: During a dependency failure, a system should keep doing what it was doing (serve last known config, keep existing capacity) rather than needing the failed dependency to recover.

principles.name: Name the guarantee, then find the mechanism
principles.body: For every invariant the business cares about (no double spend, no oversell, unique usernames), write down which mechanism enforces it: a constraint, a lock, serializable isolation or a single-writer design. "The database handles it" is not an answer.
principles.html: For every invariant the business cares about (no double spend, no oversell, unique usernames), write down which mechanism enforces it: a constraint, a lock, serializable isolation or a single-writer design. "The database handles it" is not an answer.

principles.name: Push invariants into the database
principles.body: Unique constraints, foreign keys, check and exclusion constraints, and conditional atomic updates are enforced correctly regardless of isolation level or application bugs. Application-level checks done with read-then-write are race conditions waiting for traffic.
principles.html: Unique constraints, foreign keys, check and exclusion constraints, and conditional atomic updates are enforced correctly regardless of isolation level or application bugs. Application-level checks done with read-then-write are race conditions waiting for traffic.

principles.name: Default to the strongest isolation you can afford, and measure
principles.body: Starting from serializable and relaxing per transaction with a written justification is safer than starting from Read Committed and discovering write skew in a financial audit.
principles.html: Starting from serializable and relaxing per transaction with a written justification is safer than starting from Read Committed and discovering write skew in a financial audit.

principles.name: Retries are part of the transaction contract
principles.body: Under serializable or optimistic concurrency, aborts are normal operation. Every transactional code path needs a bounded, idempotent retry wrapper, written once and shared across teams.
principles.html: Under serializable or optimistic concurrency, aborts are normal operation. Every transactional code path needs a bounded, idempotent retry wrapper, written once and shared across teams.

principles.name: Choose the storage engine for the steady-state workload, not the benchmark
principles.body: Run long enough for compaction, vacuum and checkpoints to reach equilibrium, with realistic key distributions and dataset sizes several times larger than RAM.
principles.html: Run long enough for compaction, vacuum and checkpoints to reach equilibrium, with realistic key distributions and dataset sizes several times larger than RAM.

principles.name: Durability is end-to-end
principles.body: Count acknowledged-write loss scenarios across every layer: fsync settings, replication mode, disk caches, backup cadence and failover behavior. Write the answer down as an explicit RPO, and test it.
principles.html: Count acknowledged-write loss scenarios across every layer: fsync settings, replication mode, disk caches, backup cadence and failover behavior. Write the answer down as an explicit RPO, and test it.

principles.name: Delay sharding, then shard deliberately
principles.body: Scale up, add replicas, partition tables and split services first. When you do shard, choose the key from the dominant access pattern and transaction boundaries, and build resharding tooling before you need it.
principles.html: Scale up, add replicas, partition tables and split services first. When you do shard, choose the key from the dominant access pattern and transaction boundaries, and build resharding tooling before you need it.

principles.name: Design for skew
principles.body: Assume Zipfian access patterns, giant tenants and celebrity keys. Every partitioning scheme needs a story for the 1% of keys that get 50% of the traffic.
principles.html: Assume Zipfian access patterns, giant tenants and celebrity keys. Every partitioning scheme needs a story for the 1% of keys that get 50% of the traffic.

principles.name: Failover must fence
principles.body: Promotion without guaranteed demotion of the old leader is split brain waiting to happen. Prefer consensus-based leadership, or leases with fencing tokens, over heuristics.
principles.html: Promotion without guaranteed demotion of the old leader is split brain waiting to happen. Prefer consensus-based leadership, or leases with fencing tokens, over heuristics.

principles.name: Make replication lag a first-class signal
principles.body: Expose it, alert on it, and give applications read-your-writes primitives (LSN or GTID waits, leader pinning) instead of hoping lag stays small.
principles.html: Expose it, alert on it, and give applications read-your-writes primitives (LSN or GTID waits, leader pinning) instead of hoping lag stays small.

principles.name: Garbage collection is a production service
principles.body: Vacuum, purge, compaction and tombstone cleanup need monitoring, capacity planning and owners. Long-running transactions are a resource leak and should be time-limited by policy.
principles.html: Vacuum, purge, compaction and tombstone cleanup need monitoring, capacity planning and owners. Long-running transactions are a resource leak and should be time-limited by policy.

principles.name: Plan stability beats plan optimality
principles.body: For critical queries, a predictable plan that is good enough is worth more than one that is sometimes optimal and occasionally catastrophic. Pin, hint or track plans in the places that matter.
principles.html: For critical queries, a predictable plan that is good enough is worth more than one that is sometimes optimal and occasionally catastrophic. Pin, hint or track plans in the places that matter.

principles.name: Backups don't exist until restores are tested
principles.body: Automate restore drills, measure restore time against your RTO, and verify the restored data, not just that the restore job exited zero.
principles.html: Automate restore drills, measure restore time against your RTO, and verify the restored data, not just that the restore job exited zero.

principles.name: Prefer boring, well-understood databases
principles.body: Every new engine adds failure modes your on-call engineers have never seen. The bar for introducing one should be a workload that the existing fleet demonstrably cannot serve.
principles.html: Every new engine adds failure modes your on-call engineers have never seen. The bar for introducing one should be a workload that the existing fleet demonstrably cannot serve.

principles.name: Round trips are the currency
principles.body: For anything far from the user, latency is dominated by RTT count, not bandwidth or server time. Count handshakes, redirects, DNS lookups, and sequential fetches in every critical user path, and design to remove them.
principles.html: For anything far from the user, latency is dominated by RTT count, not bandwidth or server time. Count handshakes, redirects, DNS lookups, and sequential fetches in every critical user path, and design to remove them.

principles.name: Reuse connections, but bound their lifetime
principles.body: Pooling avoids handshakes and slow start. Unbounded lifetimes break load balancing, pin traffic to stale backends, and outlive middlebox state. Set a maximum connection age with jitter, and an idle timeout shorter than any NAT or firewall on the path.
principles.html: Pooling avoids handshakes and slow start. Unbounded lifetimes break load balancing, pin traffic to stale backends, and outlive middlebox state. Set a maximum connection age with jitter, and an idle timeout shorter than any NAT or firewall on the path.

principles.name: Timeouts nest, and every call has one
principles.body: No network call without a deadline. Each layer's timeout is shorter than its caller's. Propagate deadlines (gRPC does this natively) so downstream work stops when the user has gone.
principles.html: No network call without a deadline. Each layer's timeout is shorter than its caller's. Propagate deadlines (gRPC does this natively) so downstream work stops when the user has gone.

principles.name: Retry at one layer, with a budget
principles.body: Choose one layer to own retries for each call path. Cap retries per request and as a fraction of total traffic (around 10% is a common budget). Retry only idempotent operations, with exponential backoff and jitter.
principles.html: Choose one layer to own retries for each call path. Cap retries per request and as a fraction of total traffic (around 10% is a common budget). Retry only idempotent operations, with exponential backoff and jitter.

principles.name: Health is what the client experiences
principles.body: Liveness probes check that a process exists. Readiness must reflect the ability to serve real traffic. Combine active checks with passive outlier detection, and set panic thresholds so a broken checker can't concentrate load.
principles.html: Liveness probes check that a process exists. Readiness must reflect the ability to serve real traffic. Combine active checks with passive outlier detection, and set panic thresholds so a broken checker can't concentrate load.

principles.name: Balance the unit of work you care about
principles.body: If requests vary in cost or ride multiplexed connections, balance requests at L7 or in the client, not connections at L4. Use P2C or least-request over round robin.
principles.html: If requests vary in cost or ride multiplexed connections, balance requests at L7 or in the client, not connections at L4. Use P2C or least-request over round robin.

principles.name: Design for partial failure, not binary failure
principles.body: Assume gray failure. Detect slow as well as dead. Prefer mechanisms that degrade (shed load, serve stale) over ones that cliff.
principles.html: Assume gray failure. Detect slow as well as dead. Prefer mechanisms that degrade (shed load, serve stale) over ones that cliff.

principles.name: Cache is an availability layer, not just a speed layer
principles.body: `stale-if-error`, request collapsing, and origin shields let you survive origin outages. Treat cache-key and TTL changes as production changes with load implications.
principles.html: stale-if-error, request collapsing, and origin shields let you survive origin outages. Treat cache-key and TTL changes as production changes with load implications.

principles.name: Know who caches your DNS
principles.body: TTLs are advisory. Any failover based on DNS must assume a long tail of clients on old answers. Use anycast or LB-level failover when you need seconds, not minutes.
principles.html: TTLs are advisory. Any failover based on DNS must assume a long tail of clients on old answers. Use anycast or LB-level failover when you need seconds, not minutes.

principles.name: Control planes fail static
principles.body: Proxies, sidecars, and edges must keep serving with last-known-good config when the control plane is unreachable. A control-plane outage should freeze changes, not stop traffic.
principles.html: Proxies, sidecars, and edges must keep serving with last-known-good config when the control plane is unreachable. A control-plane outage should freeze changes, not stop traffic.

principles.name: Stage config like code
principles.body: Network config (routes, mesh policy, WAF rules, CDN rules, BGP) has a blast radius equal to its reach. Canary it per cell or region with automated rollback, exactly like a binary.
principles.html: Network config (routes, mesh policy, WAF rules, CDN rules, BGP) has a blast radius equal to its reach. Canary it per cell or region with automated rollback, exactly like a binary.

principles.name: Make the client's address and identity explicit
principles.body: Carry original client IP and workload identity through every hop, trust those signals only from your own infrastructure, and authenticate service-to-service traffic with mTLS.
principles.html: Carry original client IP and workload identity through every hop, trust those signals only from your own infrastructure, and authenticate service-to-service traffic with mTLS.

principles.name: Instrument the transport
principles.body: Export retransmits, RTT, connection counts, pool saturation, DNS latency, and TLS handshake errors as first-class metrics. You can't debug what you only see in a pcap.
principles.html: Export retransmits, RTT, connection counts, pool saturation, DNS latency, and TLS handshake errors as first-class metrics. You can't debug what you only see in a pcap.

principles.name: Separate control plane from data plane
principles.body: Keep the data plane simple, statically stable, and able to run on cached configuration. Accept a lower availability target for the control plane, and never put it in the request path.
principles.html: Keep the data plane simple, statically stable, and able to run on cached configuration. Accept a lower availability target for the control plane, and never put it in the request path.

principles.name: Design for static stability
principles.body: Pre-provision enough capacity to survive the loss of an AZ (N+1 across zones) without launching anything. Recovery that requires the control plane at the moment of crisis is a recovery that may not happen.
principles.html: Pre-provision enough capacity to survive the loss of an AZ (N+1 across zones) without launching anything. Recovery that requires the control plane at the moment of crisis is a recovery that may not happen.

principles.name: Bound blast radius explicitly
principles.body: Use cells, shuffle sharding, per-tenant quotas, and progressive rollouts. Every change and every tenant should have a known maximum impact, and you should be able to state it as a number.
principles.html: Use cells, shuffle sharding, per-tenant quotas, and progressive rollouts. Every change and every tenant should have a known maximum impact, and you should be able to state it as a number.

principles.name: Prefer level-triggered reconciliation
principles.body: Controllers that compare desired state to observed state and converge are robust to missed events, restarts, and duplicates. Edge-triggered workflows that assume every event arrives exactly once are fragile.
principles.html: Controllers that compare desired state to observed state and converge are robust to missed events, restarts, and duplicates. Edge-triggered workflows that assume every event arrives exactly once are fragile.

principles.name: Requests are a contract; limits are a weapon
principles.body: Set memory requests to real working-set usage and memory limits equal to requests. Be deliberate about CPU limits. They protect neighbors, but CFS throttling damages tail latency.
principles.html: Set memory requests to real working-set usage and memory limits equal to requests. Be deliberate about CPU limits. They protect neighbors, but CFS throttling damages tail latency.

principles.name: Make shared limits visible
principles.body: Track conntrack tables, ENI/IP quotas, etcd size, API server inflight requests, NAT ports, file descriptors, and per-account API rate limits. Hidden shared limits cause the outages nobody predicted.
principles.html: Track conntrack tables, ENI/IP quotas, etcd size, API server inflight requests, NAT ports, file descriptors, and per-account API rate limits. Hidden shared limits cause the outages nobody predicted.

principles.name: Keep failure domains aligned
principles.body: Spread replicas, volumes, load balancer targets, and dependencies over the same zones. A service that is multi-AZ but whose database is single-AZ is single-AZ.
principles.html: Spread replicas, volumes, load balancer targets, and dependencies over the same zones. A service that is multi-AZ but whose database is single-AZ is single-AZ.

principles.name: Treat cross-zone and cross-region bytes as a design cost
principles.body: Data transfer pricing and latency both reward locality. Make topology an explicit input to routing and placement.
principles.html: Data transfer pricing and latency both reward locality. Make topology an explicit input to routing and placement.

principles.name: Choose isolation to match trust
principles.body: Shared-kernel containers for trusted code. gVisor or microVMs for untrusted or multi-tenant code. Hardware or account boundaries for hard tenancy and compliance.
principles.html: Shared-kernel containers for trusted code. gVisor or microVMs for untrusted or multi-tenant code. Hardware or account boundaries for hard tenancy and compliance.

principles.name: The data tier determines your RPO and RTO
principles.body: Design multi-region from the data model outward: who owns each record, how it replicates, and how you fence. Stateless failover is the easy part.
principles.html: Design multi-region from the data model outward: who owns each record, how it replicates, and how you fence. Stateless failover is the easy part.

principles.name: Exercise every recovery path
principles.body: A failover, restore, or region evacuation that hasn't been run recently should be assumed broken. Game days and continuous chaos testing turn hope into evidence.
principles.html: A failover, restore, or region evacuation that hasn't been run recently should be assumed broken. Game days and continuous chaos testing turn hope into evidence.

principles.name: Avoid synchronized behavior
principles.body: Add jitter to retries, cache expiries, cron schedules, and reconnects. Synchronized clients turn small blips into thundering herds against control planes.
principles.html: Add jitter to retries, cache expiries, cron schedules, and reconnects. Synchronized clients turn small blips into thundering herds against control planes.

probes.html: What a DE probes: "Show me the partition behavior column for your design. If region A cannot reach region B for 10 minutes, which side serves writes, and what happens to the writes the other side rejected — or worse, accepted?" A design that has no answer has not been designed; it has been assembled.

What a DE probes: "Where in this system do you compare timestamps produced by different machines, and what happens when they're wrong by 50 ms?" Any last-write-wins resolution, TTL enforcement, or cross-node lease is a place a clock bug becomes a data-loss bug.

What a DE probes: "Walk me through failover, second by second. Which writes were acknowledged but not replicated? Who decides the new leader — and what stops the old one from writing? What does the client library do during the gap?" The quality of a replication design lives entirely in its failover story.

What a DE probes: "Point to every place a request can be retried — client SDK, gateway, mesh, application, consumer. Now point to the one place that deduplicates. If there are five retry layers and zero dedup layers, this system double-charges someone eventually." Also: "What is the idempotency story for the human retry — the user who clicks Submit twice, the operator who reruns the job?"

What a DE probes: "What happens at 2× design load? Show me the specific line of code or config that says no." And the follow-up that separates real designs from hopeful ones: "When you shed, what do you shed first, and does the business agree with that ordering?" Load-shedding priority is a product decision wearing an engineering costume — surfacing that is exactly the DE's job.

probes.section: Durability: WAL, checkpoints, and what "committed" means
probes.html: Architecture review questions: "What is the durability setting on every store in the write path, including the disk cache layer beneath it — and does the acknowledged-write-loss window match what the business believes?" · "What is the measured crash-recovery time at current WAL volume, and when was it last tested with a real kill?" · "Is anything reading table state and separately publishing events (dual write), where CDC on the log would be atomic?"

Architecture review questions: "Which isolation level does each critical transaction actually run at — the configured default, not the assumed one?" · "For every invariant spanning more than one row (limits, uniqueness enforced in code, balance rules): what prevents write skew — serializable isolation, an explicit lock, or a database-checked constraint?" · "Does the data-access layer retry serialization failures and deadlock victims, with bounded attempts?" · "Any read-modify-write done as read-then-UPDATE without a version check is a lost update waiting for concurrency — where are they?"

Architecture review questions: "For the ten most critical queries: what is the plan, what keeps it stable, and what alerts if it flips?" · "Which predicates are correlated, and do extended statistics cover them?" · "What is the write cost of the index set — and which indexes have zero reads in the last 90 days?" · "Is pagination OFFSET-based (O(n) per page, drifts under writes) where keyset/seek pagination should be used?"

Architecture review questions: "Which transactions cross shard/range boundaries, at what percentage of traffic — and could the partition key make them single-shard?" · "For each saga: the compensation table (step → compensating action → what if it fails), the visibility of intermediate states, and the non-compensatable steps ordered last." · "In the multi-region topology: where are quorum members and leaseholders for each table, and what is the write latency from each region's users?"

Architecture review questions: "What is the connection strategy per hop — pool sizes, keep-alive intervals vs the smallest middlebox idle timeout on the path, and reconnect behavior with jitter?" · "Where do fresh connections sit on the hot path (cold-start latency = handshakes × RTT), and is TLS resumption enabled?" · "Any high-connection-churn component (proxy, NAT, crawler): what is the measured ephemeral-port headroom?" · "For cross-region links: which congestion control, and has BBR been evaluated against measured loss rates?"

Architecture review questions: "For gRPC/HTTP-2: where does per-request balancing happen — and if the answer is 'the NLB', expect hot backends." · "Show the health-check dependency graph: what makes readiness fail, and can a soft dependency's blip desert the fleet? Is there a fail-open panic threshold?" · "Which single layer owns retries and timeouts on each hop, and what is the worst-case multiplication if two layers both retry?" · "What happens during a rolling deploy — drain deadline, in-flight handling, and the measured error rate of a routine rollout?"

probes.section: Network failure analysis: a systematic method
probes.html: Architecture review questions: "For each hop on the golden path: what stateful limit exists (conntrack, NAT ports, flow tables, accept backlog), what is current headroom, and what alerts at 70%?" · "What is the effective MTU end-to-end across overlays/tunnels, and is MSS clamped where ICMP may be filtered?" · "Can per-path (not per-endpoint) health be observed between AZs/regions — how would an asymmetric partial partition present in the dashboards?" · "Which p99 latency modes correspond to retransmission timers, and would loss show up as latency or as errors in the SLIs?"

Architecture review questions: "Does the platform pass the static-stability test — control plane down for an hour: what actually breaks?" · "Which workloads have CPU limits, and has anyone looked at their throttling metrics next to p99?" · "What are etcd's object-count, object-size, and watch-fanout hot spots — and what protects the API server from a misbehaving client?" · "For a routine node drain: PDBs, spread constraints, and termination grace verified — what error rate does a drain actually produce?"

keyIdeas.html: You cannot distinguish slow from dead; every mechanism is a coping strategy for that.
Lower-layer reliability never removes end-to-end idempotency and reconciliation.
PACELC, not CAP: most trade-offs are latency-vs-consistency in normal operation.
Wall clocks order nothing across machines; use HLC/logical clocks, and fear LWW.
Consensus keeps safety always, liveness usually — use it narrowly, never homegrown.
Replication quality is failover quality; demand the second-by-second story and a fencing token.
Consistency is chosen per-invariant; session guarantees are the user-facing sweet spot.
Design for gray, partial, and metastable failures — crash-stop is the easy case.
Exactly-once is at-least-once plus dedup; the outbox pattern kills dual writes.
Bound every queue, budget every retry, shed early by business priority, propagate deadlines.
Every storage engine is a position on the write/read/space amplification triangle; B-trees pay at write time, LSMs at read-and-compaction time.
Committed means "commit record durably in the WAL" — and durability is a configurable chain whose weakest link (often a disk cache or an async setting) defines the real loss window.
The WAL is also the integration surface: CDC on the log replaces dual writes.
MVCC means readers and writers don't block — and that one long-lived snapshot silently poisons cleanup system-wide.
Defaults are weak: read committed / repeatable read permit lost updates and write skew, which map to real broken invariants, not textbook curiosities.
Serializability comes from 2PL, SSI, or OCC — the latter two require applications that retry aborts.
The optimizer is statistical: correlated predicates, stale statistics, and parameter skew make plan management an operational discipline, not a tuning afterthought.
2PC blocks on coordinator loss; modern systems replicate the coordinator (Spanner-class), avoid crossing shards, or decompose into sagas with real compensation design.
Distributed SQL = ranges × Raft × MVCC × 2PC-over-groups, paying quorum latency and hot-range management for regional survivability.
Boring first, one system of record per fact, and backups measured by restore drills — most database strategy is these three sentences enforced.
Every network layer is an abstraction and a failure domain; debugging maps a symptom at layer N to a mechanism at layer N−1.
Most large-scale "network problems" are state problems: connection tables, caches, and NAT mappings that go stale, exhaust, or disagree.
Handshakes cost RTTs, so pooling, keep-alives (below middlebox timeouts), and TLS resumption are structural, not optional.
Ordered channels couple the fates of multiplexed work; QUIC's per-stream independence is the pattern, and it recurs well beyond transport.
DNS is a hierarchy of caches — changes propagate at TTL speed, resolution behavior is code, and DNS steers traffic coarsely, not precisely.
L4 spreads connections; L7 spreads requests — multiplexed protocols (gRPC) need L7 or client-side balancing, or backends run hot.
Health checking needs readiness/liveness separation, passive outlier detection for gray failures, and fail-open panic behavior.
Exactly one layer owns each retry and timeout policy per hop; stacked policies multiply into self-inflicted overload.
CDN effectiveness is cache-key hygiene, immutable assets, tag-based purge, and a deliberate serve-stale posture.
Small loss rates present as quantized latency modes, not errors — retransmit counters belong on the same dashboard as p99.
Control planes decide; data planes do — and good platforms keep data planes serving on last-known-good state when control planes fail.
Everything is reconciliation: self-healing and self-reasserting misconfiguration are the same loop, so debugging means finding the controller and its input.
A container is namespaces + cgroups + layered filesystems around an ordinary process; the isolation ladder runs process → container → sandbox → VM.
CPU limits throttle (latency spikes at low average utilization); memory limits kill (exit 137); requests are the scheduling and cost currency, so their honesty is both reliability and FinOps.
etcd and the API server are the platform's shared fate: small objects, fast isolated disks, defended quotas.
Autoscalers are stacked control loops with minutes-scale actuators — headroom covers the gap, and untuned loops oscillate.
Object storage is the cloud's real shared filesystem: durable, strongly consistent, throughput-by-key-design, priced per request and per tier.
Cloud networks are software-defined state machines with metered links; cross-AZ/egress pricing and NAT/conntrack limits are architecture inputs, not billing trivia.
Buy multi-region for a named reason — latency, survivability, or residency — and prefer home-region partitioning and cells over symmetric active-active everywhere.
A DR plan's real RTO is the duration of its last successful drill.
